extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of constitutional law / political institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Explain the principles and practical limits of judicial review and the role of courts in interpreting constitutional and statutory conflicts, including how courts avoid political questions and the consequences of judicial overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to declare and apply the law
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of the courts is simply to declare and apply the law; where any court finds a law of lower authority clashing with a law of higher authority, it must reject the former as not law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies equally to State and Federal courts; when a State statute conflicts with the Federal Constitution or a Federal statute it 'must give way.' This principle is illustrated throughout the text and underpins judicial review as an ordinary judicial function (not a special extra-legal power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial annulment is a duty, not discretionary power
rubrics_metrics.description: The so‑called 'power of annulling an unconstitutional statute' is a duty rather than a power, and a duty incumbent on the humblest State court no less than on the Supreme Federal Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing emphasizes that courts do not 'grant' the right to annul but must do so when a case presents the question; it justifies judicial invalidation of subordinate enactments that exceed their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges must interpret, not control, the legislature; avoid policy judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: American judges do not 'control the legislature' but simply interpret the law; they have no concern with the motives or the results of an enactment except insofar as these throw light on legislative meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be a breach of duty for a judge to express an opinion on the policy of a statute except where policy informs meaning. Even if a judge deems a statute 'excellent' or 'pernicious,' if no constitutional power exists for it the statute must be set aside; conversely, a statute within Congress's powers must be enforced regardless of its perceived desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of judicial overreach and political mastership
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must not seek to make themselves the 'masters of the Constitution' by twisting or perverting it to suit their own political views, since such conduct would provoke public distrust and possible resistance to the law and the court itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both a normative caution and a pragmatic check: judicial legitimacy depends on restraint; overstepping risks loss of influence and public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must wait for concrete cases; do not initiate constitutional questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court does not go to meet the question; it waits for the question to come to it. When the court acts it acts at the instance of a party (often private litigants), not proactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure ensures full legal argument on both sides, delays political confrontation, and grounds constitutional decisions in private rights disputes (example: Fletcher v. Peck). It is contrasted with a hypothetical congressional veto of state laws, which would be politically inflammatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding constitutional issues in private litigation secures acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a constitutional question is decided in the course of ordinary litigation between private parties, the decision appears primarily as a judgment upon private rights and thereby obtains respect and moral support from law‑abiding citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method reduces feelings that the decision is a political attack on a State and helps avoid resistance that might follow a direct federal veto or political intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstain from adjudicating 'purely political' questions and from reviewing discretionary executive acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has declared that it is not concerned with purely political questions; where discretion is conferred on the President or an executive duty is imposed, the manner of exercise is beyond the court's province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, when the Constitution confers legislative power on Congress the court will decline to inquire into whether a particular exercise of that power was necessary or desirable — doctrines of political question and non‑reviewability of certain executive/legislative discretions limit judicial intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater need for judicial ability and integrity when interpreting broad constitutional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Constitution's words are general and lay down a few large principles, the generality of language leaves a far wider field to interpreting judges, increasing the need for ability and integrity in judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting general constitutional provisions often requires not only legal acumen but comprehension of the nature and methods of government; this elevates the importance and difficulty of judicial work compared with construing ordinary statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of federal courts in resolving conflicts between federal and state laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts created by the central authority are tasked with pronouncing whether a State law incompatible with duly enacted Federal law or the Federal Constitution must give way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This necessity arose because State courts, being offspring of State governments, might otherwise tend to uphold State laws against Federal provisions; central federal courts provide a neutral forum co‑extensive with national authority to settle such questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with systems where Parliament is sovereign (Acts cannot be invalidated)
rubrics_metrics.description: In England, judges interpret Acts of Parliament and, if they find an Act conflicting with a decided case, prefer the Act as being of higher authority; Acts cannot be declared invalid because Parliament is omnipotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights that judicial invalidation exists only where legislatures are subordinate to a superior written constitution; in systems of parliamentary sovereignty courts do not (and legally cannot) strike down statutes as invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial restraint protects dignity, impartiality, and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges, when sucked into the vortex of politics, must lose dignity, impartiality, and influence; prudence and doctrines limiting judicial engagement with politics help maintain the courts' authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates causes for the Federal courts' avoidance of political entanglement (e.g., doctrine of non‑justiciability of political questions, waiting for cases, private‑party litigation), which together sustain judicial legitimacy.
